title: Recognise and identify the basic functions of the ecological environment

lessons.title: Ecosystems and how they work
lessons.html:
What is an ecosystem?

An ecosystem is a community of living things (plants, animals, insects, fungi and bacteria) together with the non-living things around them (soil, water, air, sunlight and climate), all working together. A farm is an ecosystem too: veld, crops, livestock, wild animals, soil life, rivers and wetlands all affect each other.

Living and non-living parts

Living (biotic)Non-living (abiotic)
Grasses, trees, cropsSunlight
Cattle, goats, buck, birdsRainfall and water
Insects, earthwormsSoil minerals
Fungi, bacteriaTemperature, wind

Food chains and food webs

Energy from the sun flows through living things.

  • Producers – green plants make food from sunlight. Example: veld grass.
  • Consumers – animals that eat plants or other animals. Example: a buck eats grass (primary consumer); a jackal eats the buck (secondary consumer).
  • Decomposers – fungi, bacteria and earthworms break down dead plants, dung and dead animals and return nutrients to the soil.

A food chain shows one path: grass to grasshopper to bird to snake. A food web shows how many chains link together. If one link is removed, for example if all the owls and snakes are killed, rats and mice can increase and damage crops and stored grain.

South African biomes

South Africa has several biomes, large areas with similar climate and vegetation: grassland (much of the Highveld), savanna (bushveld of Limpopo and Mpumalanga), Nama Karoo and Succulent Karoo (dry west), fynbos (Western Cape), forest, thicket and desert. Farming methods must suit the biome. Grazing that works in high-rainfall grassland could badly damage the Karoo.

lessons.title: Natural cycles and the services nature provides
lessons.html:
Natural cycles

The water cycle

  1. Water evaporates from dams, rivers, soil and the sea, and plants release water through their leaves.
  2. Water vapour rises, cools and forms clouds.
  3. Rain or hail falls.
  4. Water soaks into the soil and groundwater, or runs off into streams, rivers and dams.

Good plant cover helps rain soak in. Bare, trampled soil lets water run off fast, causing erosion and less water stored in the soil.

The nutrient cycle

Plants take nutrients from the soil. Animals eat the plants. Dung, urine, dead leaves and dead animals are broken down by decomposers, and the nutrients go back into the soil. Burning all crop residues or removing all dung breaks this cycle.

The carbon cycle

Plants take carbon dioxide from the air to build their bodies. When plants and animals respire, rot or are burned, carbon dioxide returns to the air. Healthy soils with plenty of organic matter store carbon.

Ecosystem services

Healthy ecosystems provide services that farms depend on:

  • Pollination by bees and other insects for fruit, vegetables and seed crops.
  • Clean water filtered by wetlands and vegetation along rivers.
  • Soil formation and fertility through decomposers.
  • Natural pest control by birds, spiders, ladybirds, owls and other predators.
  • Grazing from veld.
  • Protection from floods and erosion by wetlands and plant cover.

Human impact

Overgrazing, ploughing steep slopes, draining wetlands, spreading alien plants such as wattle and pollution with chemicals or waste damage these functions. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 and the National Water Act 36 of 1998 help protect soil, veld and water.

Key points

  • An ecosystem is living things plus their non-living environment, working together.
  • Energy flows from producers to consumers; decomposers recycle nutrients.
  • Water, nutrient and carbon cycles keep the farm productive.
  • Nature provides services such as pollination, clean water and pest control.
  • Overgrazing, wetland drainage and alien plants damage ecosystem functions.
